statements.claim: Krishna thought of Narada and the sage arrived as soon as he was thought of.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'as soon as he was thought of by Krishna, that foremost of Munis... Nārada... arrived there'.

statements.claim: At the appointed hour Krishna and Satyabhama bathed the great muni Narada, anointed him with scents and garlands and fed him, honouring him for the Punyaka ceremonies.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'when the appointed hour came, the eternal Vāsudeva... along with the beloved Satyā... worshipped the great Muni Nārada... with scents and garlands and fed him'. Pack title itself is 'Satyabhama's Punyaka Rite'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama bound Krishna to the Parijata tree with a garland of flowers and, with his permission, dedicated him to Narada.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'the lucky damsel, having put a garland of flowers around Krishna's neck, bound him to the Pārijāta tree... obtaining his permission she dedicated Keshava unto Nārada'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama gave away sesame seeds gleaming like jewels, gold mixed with rice and other plants, mountains of gold, and a thousand cows.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'she gave away sessamum seeds illumined with the lustre of jems and jewels, gold mixed with rice and other plants, mountains of gold and a thousand kine'.

statements.claim: Narada accepted everything and told Krishna that, given by Satya with water, he had become his, ordering him to follow and obey; Krishna replied 'This is the first stage' and followed.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'given by Satya together with water thou hast become mine. Do thou follow me and do what I say.' ... Janārddana said 'This is the first stage' and began to follow Nārada.

statements.claim: Narada cut jokes, said 'do thou wait here, I shall go', took the garland from Krishna's neck and demanded a Kapila cow with a calf and a black-antelope skin full of sesame seeds and gold as the fee of release, a means laid down by the god whose emblem is the bull (Shiva).
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): verbatim verses 11-13, including 'This means of release has been laid down by the god (Siva) having a bull for his emblem'.

statements.claim: Krishna said 'So be it', offered the fee, then smilingly offered Narada a boon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Janārddana said "So be it" and offered him the same fee of release... Pray for a desired-for boon and I will grant it'.

statements.claim: Narada asked that Vishnu always remain pleased with him and grant him habitation with him, and that any rebirth be as a Brahmana born of no woman; Krishna granted it.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): verses 16-18 verbatim; 'the Lord Vishnu said "So it will be"'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama had invited all sixteen thousand wives of Krishna to the Punyaka ceremony and, at its close, distributed among them the celestial garments and ornaments Shachi had previously given to Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Satyabhāmā... had invited... the sixteen thousand wives of the highly powerful Vishnu. And at the termination of the ceremony she distributed amongst them all those celestial raiments and ornaments which Sachi had previously given to Vāsudeva'.

statements.claim: The Parijata, at Krishna's command, displayed its own accomplishments while friends and relations invited by Narada and Keshava witnessed its power.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Living there, Pārijāta, at the command of Vāsudeva, began to display its own accomplishments... all their friends and relations began to witness the power of Pārijāta'.

statements.claim: Krishna brought the Pandavas with Pritha, Draupadi and Subhadra; Shrutasrava came with her son and Bhishmaka with his, along with other friends and relations.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'the highly powerful Hari had brought there the Pandavas along with Prithā, Draupadi, and Subhadrā... Shrutasravā, with her son, Bhishmaka with his son and other friends and relations were also brought there'.

statements.claim: For a year Krishna stayed happily in Dwaraka with Arjuna and the ladies of his household; at the end of that year he returned the Parijata to the city of the celestials.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'after a year had elapsed the highly powerful Keshava... returned with Pārijāta to the city of the celestials and saluted Sakra, Aditi, and Kashyapa'.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims. The pack passage supports every named event, quote, and number. The opening line's framing ('all within the same afternoon', garland as binding/ransom) is atmosphere over a rite the passage narrates continuously; the pack title itself frames it as 'Satyabhama's Punyaka Rite'.

statements.claim: Recap: the battle over the Parijata had ended only when Kashyapa and Aditi, sent by Brahma, halted it and the two 'brothers' bathed in the Jahnvi and made peace.
statements.evidence: Prior-story summary carried in the DKS_0234 pack chain: 'Kashyapa and Aditi Reconcile Krishna and Indra || Sent by Brahma, the parents Kashyapa and Aditi halt the battle, and the two "brothers" lay down their arms, bathe in the Jahnvi, and are reconciled'. Aditi's words in this pack ('may you both always entertain such a brotherly feeling') confirm the fraternal frame.

statements.claim: After a year of festival Krishna carried the Parijata from Dwaraka up to heaven and saluted Indra (Sakra), Aditi and Kashyapa.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'after a year had elapsed... Keshava... returned with Pārijāta to the city of the celestials and saluted Sakra, Aditi, and Kashyapa'.

statements.claim: Aditi, after Krishna bowed to her, asked that the two always keep brotherly feeling and that Krishna satisfy this desire; he said 'It shall be so'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): verses 28-29 verbatim ('may you both always entertain such a brotherly feeling... It shall be so').

statements.claim: Krishna told Indra he had been commanded by the high-souled Shiva to destroy all the unslayable Danavas living on earth and would kill all those Asuras within ten days.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'I have been commanded by the high-souled Siva, to destroy all the unslayable Dānavas living on earth. From to-day within ten days I will kill all those Asuras'.

statements.claim: Krishna said Pravara with the heroic Jayanta must wait in the sky at the time of the battle to slay the Danavas, one of them a god in human form and the other the son of a god.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Pravara, together with the heroic Jayanta, shall have to wait in the sky for slaying those Dānavas. Of them one is a god in a human form and the other is the son of a god'.

statements.claim: Krishna explained the Danavas, proud of Brahma's boon, were unslayable by the gods, but he would kill them 'for I am now a man'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Although those Dānavas, proud of the boon conferred on them by Brahmā, are unslayable by the gods, still we will kill them for I am now a man'. Also the pack's evidence excerpt, verbatim.

statements.claim: Indra, pleased, said 'So it will be', and he and Krishna embraced each other.
statements.evidence: HV 1.223 (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937): 'Then Indra, pleased, said to Krishna "So it will be." And then... they embraced each other'.

statements.claim: Connective reflections — that Krishna's human form was his weapon against a boon that shielded the Danavas from every god, and that the ten days had begun to run unknown to the world below.
statements.evidence: Exegesis of the quoted vow; the pack confirms the boon from Brahma and the ten-day promise but does not itself editorialize.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims. The pack passage (HV 1.223) carries the entire scene verbatim; dialogue quotes in the story match. Note: the opening recap of the earlier Parijata battle is verified against the previous-story summary in the DKS_0234 pack chain, not against this pack's own passage.

statements.claim: The inhabitants of Shatpura, Nikumbha and other Daityas, proud of their boon, assembled and demanded: 'Give us our share in the Yajna. We will drink Soma and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters', plus his most valuable jewels, threatening not to allow the yajna if he transgressed.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): verses 6-12 quoted nearly verbatim, incl. 'If he transgresses this order we will not allow him to celebrate this Yajna. This is our order'.

statements.claim: The setting was the city of Shatpura on the sacred bank of the river Avarta, resorted to by munis, where the Vajasaneyi Brahmana Brahmadatta, a disciple of Yajnavalkya, well-read in the four Vedas and six Angas and endued with morality, was initiated into a yajna extending over a year.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): verses 1-3, including 'Brahmadatta, a disciple of Yajnawalka, well-read in the four Vedas and six Angas and endued with morality, was initiated into a Yajna extending over a year'.

statements.claim: Brahmadatta answered that no portion of sacrificial offerings was laid down for them in the Vedas (they could ask the assembled munis), that he would give his daughters to proper bridegrooms following the Vedas, and that if they came to terms he might give his entire collection of jewels but if they used force he would give nothing, 'for Devaki's son is my supporter'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): verses 13-16 nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The Danavas chose force: they scattered the articles of the yajna and began carrying away his daughters.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'the wicked Dānavas of Shatpura, Nikumbha and others began to scatter the articles of Yajna and carry away his daughters'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva and Devaki were at Shatpura because Brahmadatta was a class-friend and preceptor of Vasudeva, and Vasudeva had come with Devaki to protect him, as Indra guards Brihaspati, his own preceptor.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'as Sakra... protects Vrihaspati so... Vasudeva, with Devaki, repaired there for protecting him, for he was a class friend and preceptor of Anakadundubhi (Vasudeva)'.

statements.claim: At the yajna were present the munis Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritiman, Jajali, Devala and others of firm devotion, and Devaki distributed among the beggars whatever each wanted, proportionate to Vasudeva's wealth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'were present Vyasa, Yajnawalka, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritimān, Jajali, Devala and other great and leading Munis of firm devotion... the pious Devaki distributed amongst the beggars various articles they wanted proportionate to the wealth of the intelligent Vasudeva'.

statements.claim: Seeing the sacrificial articles robbed by the Asuras, Vasudeva thought of Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada, and as soon as he was thought of Krishna came to know everything.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'Anakadundubhi thought of the great Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. As soon as he was thought of Krishna came to know of every thing'.

statements.claim: Krishna ordered Pradyumna to proceed and save the maidens by his illusive powers, saying he himself would soon go to Shatpura with the Yadava army.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'Proceed, O my son, and save the maidens by virtue of your illusive powers... I myself too will soon go to Shatpura with the Yādava army'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, ever obedient, went within a moment, took away the maidens by illusion, created illusory figures which he left before the Daityas, and told Devaki 'Be not afraid'; the Daityas carried off the illusory maidens and entered their city with satisfaction while Brahmadatta's real daughters were safe.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): verses 17-23 nearly verbatim ('leaving aside Brahmadatta's daughter the irrepressible Daityas carried away the illusory maidens and entered their city with satisfaction').

statements.claim: The great yajna continued according to proper rites, and all the kings invited by Brahmadatta — Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the Malava and Tangana kings, Rukmi, Ahvriti, Neela, Narmada, Vinda, Anuvinda, Avantya, Shalya, Shakuni and others — arrived and encamped near Shatpura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'that great and glorious Yajna was being celebrated according to proper rites... all the kings, invited by the intelligent Brahmadatta, arrived at the sacrificial ground... encamped near Shatpura' (name list verbatim).

statements.claim: The sacrifice now wore a ring of armies around it — 'and the year was not yet half done', with every new arrival making the encampment thicker.
statements.evidence: No pack passage states how far the year-long yajna had progressed when the kings encamped; the pack says only that the yajna was 'extending over a year' and that the kings arrived and encamped. The visible passage (and its excerpt) contains no elapsed-time figure.

corrections.original_sentence: The sacrifice that had begun as a year of offerings now wore a ring of armies around it — and the year was not yet half done, and every new arrival made the encampment thicker and the air heavier.
corrections.suggested: The sacrifice that had begun as a year of offerings now wore a ring of armies around it, and every new arrival made the encampment thicker and the air heavier.

notes: 1 UNSUPPORTED (the 'year was not yet half done' timing claim — the pack gives no elapsed-time figure; kings simply 'encamped near Shatpura' while the year-long yajna went on). Everything else is verbatim-supported, including dialogue and the king list. Passages truncated mid-chapter ('[...]' markers) in the pack did not affect these claims.

statements.claim: Narada's quoted thought: 'At this Yajna all the Kshatriyas and the Yadavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'Seeing this the beautiful Nārada thought:—"At this Yajna all the Kshatryas and Yādavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about." Thinking this he repaired to Nikumbha's house'.

statements.claim: The assembled kings (Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the Malava and Tangana kings, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni and more) camped around the sacrificial ground where Brahmadatta's year-long rite burned, with the Yadavas on the other side.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): king list and 'encamped near Shatpura' (verses 24-28). The Yadava presence at the ground follows from the same chapter and from ch. 231's 'the Pandavas in charge of the Yajna'.

statements.claim: Framing gloss: in the city the Danavas nursed the grievance of the maidens they had thought to carry off.
statements.evidence: Motive/state-of-mind framing, not a stated source fact. The same chapter says the Daityas carried away the illusory maidens and 'entered their city with satisfaction', so the 'nursed a grievance' gloss is the story's interpretation (they never obtained the real daughters, which is the seed of the dissension Narada refers to).

statements.claim: The Danavas received Narada with worship and seated him; he asked Nikumbha how he could sit at ease after causing a dissension with the Yadavas, since Brahmadatta was the friend of Krishna's father.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): 'He was worshipped there by Nikumbha and other Dānavas... Having caused a dissension with the Yadavas how are you sitting here at ease? Do you not know that Brahmadatta is the friend of Krishna's father?'

statements.claim: Narada told Nikumbha that Brahmadatta's five hundred wives had been brought to the sacrificial ground (200 of Brahmana origin, 100 Kshatriya, 100 Vaishya, 100 Shudra); all had worshipped Durvasa, who booned that each would get a son and a daughter one by one, and by that boon they had all given birth to fair daughters of matchless beauty, tender, ever youthful, chaste, fragrant with the scent of all flowers.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt): verses 33-38 verbatim, including the varna breakdown (200/100/100/100) and Durvasa's boon.

statements.claim: Narada drew the conclusion that jewels would open the ears of the kings and maidens would seal the bargain (the Asuras were to win the assembled kings with jewels and maidens).
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'Narada... prompts the Asuras to bribe the assembled kings with jewels and maidens so they will fight the Yadavas'. Pack excerpt: Nārada tells Nikumbha 'O hero, you invite in proper order the help of other kings'. (Passage itself truncates at verse ~38.)

statements.claim: Narada urged Nikumbha to invite, in proper order, the help of the other kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: 'O hero, you invite in proper order the help of other kings'.

statements.claim: Returning through the encampment, Narada prevented the heroic sons of Pandu, holding the Pandavas back so they would not stand with the Yadavas when trouble came.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: '...returning... the great Nārada prevented the heroic sons of Pandu'. Consistent with ch. 231 where 'the Pandavas [are] in charge of the Yajna' rather than on the battlefield.

statements.claim: Closing stage-setting: the Danavas had allies among the kings, and everything had been arranged for a battle without Narada raising his voice.
statements.evidence: Summary/connective restatement of the incitement; no new factual assertion.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims. One connective-narration question: the gloss that the Danavas 'nursed the grievance of the maidens they had thought to carry off' — interpretive, since the pack has them satisfied with the illusory maidens. All substantive claims (Narada's incitement, the 500 wives' varna breakdown, Durvasa's boon, inviting the kings' help, preventing the Pandavas) are supported by the passage or the pack's own summary/excerpt where the passage is truncated.

statements.claim: At sunrise the Danavas came out of Shatpura roaring, on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises, many chariots drawn by the same beasts, with the sound of trumpets, car wheels and conches.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'Within a moment of the clear sun coming within the range of people's vision... the Dānavas... came out of Shatpura... on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises. Many of their cars were drawn by those animals... the sound of trumpets, rattle of car wheels, and the blowing of conches'.

statements.claim: Krishna, Baladeva and Satyaki rode to the field on Garuda's back, bathed in the waters of the sacred river Avarta, and worshipped Shiva before the battle.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'Baladeva, Krishna and Satyaki delightedly got upon Garuda's back. Having bathed in the water of the sacred river Avarta... worshipped the god Siva'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna stood at the head of the army, the Pandavas were in charge of the yajna (guarding the sacrifice ground), and remaining soldiers were at the door of the cave; Jayanta and Pravara were summoned by Krishna's thought, arrived instantly, were visible only to Krishna, and were kept above.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'having placed Pradyumna above in front of the army, the Pandavas in charge of the Yajna and the remaining soldiers at the door of the cave... thought of Jayanta and Pravara... they arrived there as soon as they were recollected. The Lord only could see them and they were kept above along with Pradyumna'.

statements.claim: At Krishna's mandate war-bugles and other instruments were sounded; Samba and Gada arranged the soldiers in the shape of a makara (crocodile-like sea monster), and Sharana, Uddhava, Viprithu, Prithu, Sudangshthra, Vichakshu and others helped Aniruddha protect the rear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'at Krishna's mandate, war-bugles... were sounded... Sāmva and Gada arranged the soldiers in the shape of a Makara. Shārana, Uddhava... Viprithu, Prithu... Sudangsthra, Vichakshu... began to help Aniruddha and protect the rear of the army'. ('Makara' glossed as 'great crocodile' is a standard rendering.)

statements.claim: The kings siding with the Asuras included the followers of the Chedi king Shishupala, the hundred brothers headed by Duryodhana, and Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni and Jarasandha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'the soldiers of the Chedi and other kings were bent upon assisting the Asuras... amongst the followers of the Chedi king Shishupāla, the hundred brothers headed by Duryodhana stood there... the king Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarāsandha... got themselves ready for the encounter'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha came out at the head of the Asura army as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host so Nikumbha came out at the head of that Asura army'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha assailed the Yadava army with arrows like serpents; Anadhrishti, commander-in-chief of the Yadu army, could not bear it and answered shaft for shaft until everything was covered with arrows and Nikumbha, his chariot, standard and horses became invisible; seeing this, the foremost of the illusory-possessed was filled with anger.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'Nikumbha began to assail the dreadful army of the Bhaimas with arrows like serpents, Anādhristhi, the commander-in-chief of the Yadu army, could not bear it... when everything was covered with arrows, Nikumbha, his chariot, standard and horses became invisible. Seeing it the heroic Nikumbha... was filled with anger'.

statements.claim: By his illusive powers Nikumbha bewildered Anadhrishti, carried him to the cave named Shatpura and imprisoned him, then returned and took Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana of Bhoja's race, Sanatkumar, Arksha (Jambavati's son), Nishatha, Ulmukha and numerous other Yadavas one by one into the dreadful cave, so covering himself that no one could see him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): verses 27-29 nearly verbatim; 'when he led the Yadavas to the dreadful cave of Shatpura he so covered himself by his illusive powers that no body could see him'.

statements.claim: Krishna, Baladeva, Satyaki, Samba, the irrepressible Aniruddha, Pradyumna especially, and many other Yadavas were filled with anger at the onslaught.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'the Lord Krishna, Baladeva, Sātyaki, Sāmva, the slayer of inimical heroes, the irrepressible Aniruddha and numerous other Bhaimas, especially Pradyumna, were greatly filled with anger'.

statements.claim: Krishna set string to his Sarnga bow and began to move among the Danavas as the god of fire ranges on grass.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'setting string to his Srānga bow and shooting arrows the holder of the Srānga (Krishna) began to move about amongst the Dānavas as the god of fire ranges on grass'.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims and no connective questions. All characters, mounts, formations, ally lists, the imprisonment sequence and the Sarnga image map verbatim to HV 1.231. 'Great crocodile' for makara and the 'war fought by subtraction' passages are imagery, not sourceable facts.

statements.claim: Anadhrishti and the other captains had been swallowed into the cave of Shatpura one by one through Nikumbha's illusion, so the Yadava army's heart was inside the mountain.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'bewildering Anadhristhi and bringing him to the cave named Shatpura the heroic Nikumbha imprisoned him there... took there Kritavarmā... Nishatha, Ulmuku and numerous other Yādavas' (verses 27-29, present in this pack's passage).

statements.claim: With the Sarnga strung, Krishna moved among the Danavas as fire ranges over dry grass, his arrows flying before him in sheets.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'setting string to his Srānga bow and shooting arrows the holder of the Srānga (Krishna) began to move about amongst the Dānavas as the god of fire ranges on grass'.

statements.claim: The Danavas took up thousands of sataghnis, parighas, fiery lances and burning axes, tore up dreadful rocks and great stones, hurled infuriated elephants, chariots and horses, and ran at Krishna like locusts driven by the noose of Death into a burning fire.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'taking up thousands of Sataghnis, Parighas, fiery lances, burning axes, dreadful rocks, and huge stones and throwing up infuriated elephants, cars and horses the Danavas ran towards the effulgent god as the locusts, drawn by the noose of Death, run towards the burning fire'.

statements.claim: The Narayana-fire consumed all those weapons, stones, elephants and chariots, and the smiling Krishna baffled them all with the fire of his arrows, standing like a bull suffering an autumn downpour.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt): 'Narayana-fire consumed all those things. And smiling the highly effulgent Yadu chief... baffled them all with the fire of his arrows. And as a bull suffers the downpour of rain in the autumn so he bore the shower [of weapons]'.

statements.claim: As soon as any Asura rose into the sky, Jayanta and Pravara — summoned by Krishna's thought before the battle and visible only to him — met them with arrows and every one fell.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: 'as soon as they rose up into the sky Jayanta and Pravara killed them all with arrows'; the pair's summoning and stationing above is in verses 1-6 of the same chapter (in this pack's passage).

statements.claim: The Danava host was routed and burned; the rout Nikumbha's illusion had postponed came in full, and the cave of Shatpura still held its prisoners.
statements.evidence: The rout of the Asuras continues into ch. 232 ('Completely routed by Krishna... the heroes fled away on all sides' — DKS_0240 pack); the imprisoned Yadava heroes in the Shatpura cave are per ch. 231 verses 27-29. 'The cave was not [won]' is connective.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims. Similes and mood ('smiling since he strung the bow', 'the sky became a wall') are imagery over supported events. The pack passage truncates at verse ~36 ('[...]') but the sky-slaying claim is carried by the pack's own evidence excerpt.

statements.claim: When the kings and their followers were imprisoned, fear entered the minds of the Asuras; completely routed by Krishna and the Yadavas, the heroes fled on all sides.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'when the kings, with their followers, were imprisoned fear entered into the mind of the Asuras. Completely routed by Krishna, Anarta and other Yadavas... the heroes fled away on all sides'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha rebuked the fleeing host: they broke their promise to avenge their slain kinsmen; heroes slain in battle live happily in the region of the celestials, while cowards must face their wives at home — 'Shame on you'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): Nikumbha's speech (verses 1-6) closely paraphrased; 'Why do ye... break your promise and take to your heels? You promised to avenge the destruction of your kinsmen... If you however fly away whose face will you behold in your house? What will your wives say? Oh fie on you!'

statements.claim: The Asuras, filled with shame, returned with double vigour and engaged the Yadavas again; Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva destroyed all who went to the sacrificial ground.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'the Asuras, filled with shame, returned with double vigour and again engaged in an encounter with the Yādavas. Dhananjaya, Bhima, Nakula, Sahadeva and Dharma's son, the king Yudhishthira destroyed all who went to that sacrificial ground'.

statements.claim: Those who rose up into the sky were slain by Indra's son (Jayanta) and the foremost of the twice-born Pravara, still on watch above the field.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'Those, who rose up into the sky, were slain by Indra's son and the foremost of the twice-born Pravara'. The story's naming of Indra's son as Jayanta follows the pair's identity established in ch. 223/231.

statements.claim: A river of blood flowed down from the mountain Govinda, its fishes the swords of the fallen.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'there flew a river of blood... It took its rise from the mountain Govinda and its water was the blood of the Asuras... The swords were the fishes'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha leaped up and fought on; Jayanta and Pravara met him with thunderbolt-like arrows; he struck Pravara down with his parigha (iron club); Indra's son caught Pravara, embraced him, found him alive, set him down, then wounded Nikumbha's person with numerous shafts.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): verses 13-19 closely followed; 'Nikumbha struck Pravara with his Parigha who fell down on earth. As soon as he fell down Indra's son held him up and embraced him with his arms. Knowing him alive he at once let him off and ran towards the Asura... Indra's son wounded Nikumbha's person with numerous shafts'.

statements.claim: The wounded Nikumbha, thinking of Krishna who had killed his kinsmen, broke off the fight and vanished, going to where Krishna stood.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'the great Asura thought:—"I shall fight in the battle-field with my enemy Krishna who has killed my kinsmen..."... Nikumbha disappeared from that place and went where the highly powerful Krishna was'.

statements.claim: Indra, seated on Airavata, came down with the gods to witness the battle; pleased with his victorious son, he embraced him and Pravara (freed from stupefaction) and had celestial trumpets sounded.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt): 'Seated on his Airāvata the virtuous destroyer of Bala, Vāsava, had come there with the gods to witness the battle... he embraced him and Pravara who was freed from stupifaction... celestial trumpets were struck at the command of the king of gods'.

statements.claim: When the last Asura had fallen or fled the war was over, and Krishna gave the victory away: the captive kings were brought before him and instead of punishment received jewels and fine raiment from his hand.
statements.evidence: Pack summary/index: 'After the victory, Krishna gives the Daitya maidens to the Yadavas, jewels and raiment to the kings, six thousand chariots to the Pandavas, and the city of Shatpura to Brahmadatta'. (Passage truncated at verse 33 before the distribution scene.)

statements.claim: To the Yadavas Krishna gave the hundreds of Daitya maidens of the conquered city; to the Pandavas he gave six thousand chariots with their horses.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: 'Keshava... conferred upon the Yadavas hundreds of Daitya maidens... he gave the Pāndavas six thousand cars with horses'.

statements.claim: In conquered Shatpura there lived the brahmana Brahmadatta (the yajna-performer of ch. 230), and Krishna summoned him and granted him the city itself, caves and walls and all.
statements.evidence: HV 1.232 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: 'gave that city of Shatpura to the Brāhmana Brahmadatta'; ch. 230 (this story's lineage) establishes Brahmadatta the Vajasaneyi Brahmana in Shatpura.

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims. Story compresses the sequel (Nikumbha's renewed attack on Krishna/Arjuna, verses 24-33 and beyond, dealt with in later stories) into 'the war was over'; the pack's own summary frames the distribution as 'after the victory', so no assertion contradicts the pack. The ch. 232 passage in the pack is truncated ('[...]') before the spoils scene; spoils are supported by the pack summary + evidence excerpt.

statements.claim: After the battles the Yadavas took to the sea, and Balarama, drunk on Kadamvari wine with reddened eyes, fair as the moon in cloud-dark raiment, sported with Revati, daughter of King Revata, delighted by looking at her face.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'Having lost all control over himself... for drinking Kadamvari wine and with his eyes reddened the highly beautiful Bala... began to sport with Revati... clad in raiments black like clouds the divine Rāma, fair like the rays of the moon... attained to an excess of delight by repeatedly looking at the countenance of his beloved consort'. Arjuna 'had come there for the sea-voyage' confirms the maritime setting.

statements.claim: At Krishna's command the beautiful Apsaras came to please Rama and Revati; dressed as the women of the Yadava country, they saluted Revati and Rama, danced in time with gestures expressive of every emotion, and sang, in the Yadava tongue, songs set to thousands of tunes.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'at the command of Keshava... the beautiful Apsaras approached... saluted Revati and Rāma and began to dance in accompaniment with time... Having dressed themselves after the women of the country of the Yādavas those... damsels sang, in their language, songs set to thou sands of tunes'.

statements.claim: The songs recounted Krishna's deeds: the destruction of Kamsa, Pralamba and Chanura; the tying to the mortar that earned the name Damodara; Putana's destruction; the uprooting of the two trees; Kaliya pressed down in the lake; Govardhana upheld for Gokula; the hump-backed woman cured; the dwarfish form assumed; the wolves created; Saubha slain; Subhadra carried away; the battle with Valahaka and Jamvumali; and the jewels carried off in Indra's very presence.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): verses 7-14 enumerate all of these nearly item for item ('destruction of Kansa, Pralamva, and Chanura... tied to the mortar... obtained the name of Damodara... destruction of Putana... uprooting of the trees Yamala and Arjuna... creation of wolves... suppression of the wicked king of serpents Kalya by Krishna in the lake... upholding of the mount Govardhana for the benefit of Gokula... cured the hump-backed woman... assumed the most wretched dwarfish form... how Soubha was slain... the carrying away of Subhdrā; the battle with Vālāhaka and Jamvumāli; and how he carried away all the jewels in the very presence of Sakra after defeating him').

statements.claim: Balarama, drunk with Kadamvari wine, sang with his wife Revati with sweet clapping of hands; Krishna, to please his brother, sang with Satyabhama.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'the highly beautiful Balarāma, drunk with Kadamvari wine, began to sing with his wife Revati accompanied with sweet clapping of hands... Madhusudana, in order to please him, began to sing with Satya'.

statements.claim: Arjuna, who had come for the sea-voyage, joined his sister Subhadra and Krishna in singing; Gada, Sarana, Pradyumna, Samba, Satyaki, Charudeshna, Rama's sons Nishatha and Ulmukha, the commander Akrura, Sankha and other leading Yadavas sang in a chorus.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'Pārtha, who had come there for the sea-voyage, also delightedly joined the beautiful Subhadrā and Krishna in their singing... Gada, Sārana, Pradyumna, Shāmva, Satyaki... Chārudeshna also sang there in a chorus. Rāma's sons... Nishatha and Ulmukha, the commander, Akrura, Sankha and other leading Bhaimas also sang there'.

statements.claim: By Krishna's power the boats increased in size, and when the Yadu chiefs sang the whole world was filled with joy and sins were dissipated.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'by Krishna's power the boats increased in size and Janarddana sang to his best along with the leading Bhaimas... the whole world was filled with joy and sins were dissipated'.

statements.claim: Narada, the guest of the celestials, sang for Krishna with such intensity that a portion of his matted hair melted away; composing the songs on the spot, he sang them again and again with various gestures and motions.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'Narada, the guest of the celestials, began to sing in such a way amongst the Yadavas that a portion of his matted hairs melted away... composing the songs there and then, that Muni... sang them amongst the Bhaimas again and again with various gestures and motions'.

statements.claim: Narada smiled on Baladeva, Revata's daughter, Krishna, Pritha's son Arjuna, Satyabhama and Subhadra; though Krishna's wives were patient by nature, the joking sage made them laugh; he sang tunes high and low, laughed aloud and shed tears of joy.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'beholding Baladeva, the daughter of the king Revata, Keshava, Pritha's son, Satyabhānā and Subhadrā, the intelligent Rishi smiled repeatedly. Although the wives of Keshava were patient by nature still the intelligent Nārada, ever fond of joking... made them laugh... sang various tunes high and low... began to laugh aloud and shed tears of joy'.

statements.claim: Krishna danced: to the music of his own flute he performed the Hallishaka before them all, and the Apsaras answered him, the beautiful Rambha rising to dance before Rama and Keshava, with Urvashi.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt) pack evidence excerpt: 'Narada began to play on his Vinā... Krishna began to perform Hallishaka accompanied with the music of his flute... the beautiful Rambhā... rose up, played and pleased Rāma and Keshava'. Urvashi is named alongside Rambha as a performer in the pack's own index entry/summary.

statements.claim: The celestial song called the Chhalikya, previously heard only in heaven, was brought down that day and sung for mankind.
statements.evidence: Pack title and summary: 'Krishna Brings the Celestial Chhalikya Song to the Yadavas... the celestial Chhalikya song is brought down for mankind'. ('Heard only in heaven' is the natural gloss on 'celestial'.) Passage truncated ('[...]') before this scene.

statements.claim: When the music ended, the damsels at Krishna's command gave away the best jewels of the world, beautiful raiments and garlands, until every guest was laden with gifts.
statements.evidence: HV 1.236 (Dutt): 'the youthful damsels, conversant with gestures, gave away, at Krishna's command, the best jewels of the world, beautiful raiments, garlands made in hea[ven]...' (passage truncates mid-verse; the giving is verbatim in the visible text).

notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims and no connective questions. Every detail — Balarama and Revati, the Apsaras' dress and dance, the catalogue of Krishna's deeds in song, the singers, the swelling boats, Narada's melting locks and laughter, the Hallishaka and Rambha/Urvashi, the Chhalikya, the gift-giving — maps verbatim to HV 1.236 or the pack's summary/excerpt where the passage is truncated. One map note: 'in the Yadava tongue' glosses the pack's 'in their language'; harmless.
